speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MR. DREW    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. An hour before the house opened the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence gave very important statements to the press which I think should have been given in the house while the house is sitting. I think the announcement of the retirement of Lieutenant General Guy Simonds is something that should have been announced here.
I think also that the announcement of the appointment of Air Marshal Miller as the new deputy minister of national defence is something that should have been made here. These are matters of concern to the members of this house. There are other appointments which I need not mention of considerable importance also dealt with in these statements.
We are sitting here doing the business of the people of Canada. These appointments affect very important aspects of the affairs of Canada. Naturally, at a time when the house is not sitting there is no choice but to make these statements to the press in the ordinary way. But I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is treating the members of this house with scant courtesy to announce an hour in advance of our meeting here information of this importance. As the people's representatives we 50433-286
are permitted to obtain our information through the press at second hand, which we should have obtained here. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is a practice which should be discontinued, and that this offers another example of the disregard both of the dignity and the responsibility of parliament which should not be overlooked.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MR. DREW    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I thank the Leader of the Opposition for the tone of his remarks. Perhaps this is a practice that should be discontinued, but it is one that has been in existence since the beginning of this parliament some 88 years ago. These appointments have always been announced when they were made, and up to the present it has not been felt they should not be disclosed until they could first be announced to the house. But I am sure that so far as I am concerned, and so far as all of my predecessors and their colleagues are concerned, there never has been any intention of being discourteous to the members of the house. We will, of course, take very seriously these remarks by the Leader of the Opposition, and we will consider whether a change should be made in the matter of reporting to the house, before the public is informed of the usual permutations that take place in the civil service, even when it has become apparent that, either through speculation or otherwise, there has already been publicity in the press about the probability of their being made.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF WITHDRAWAL OF GOVERNMENT SUPPORT
speechtext:
I wish to make an announcement about the government's decision regarding the future of the Canadian international trade fair.
The trade fair was established by the government at the end of the war to promote Canadian trade. It was hoped that Canadian producers would take advantage of the opportunity to exhibit their wares to buyers from other lands. Equally important, it was hoped that the people from other lands, particularly from overseas countries which were striving to reconstruct their war-shattered economies, would use the fair to re-establish themselves in the Canadian market. This was to be a truly international trade fair, based on the principle that trade is a two-way street.
In many respects the Canadian international trade fair has been an outstanding success. I am sure those hon. members of the house who have visited the eighth fair now being held in Toronto will bear me out as to the excellence of the administrative arrangements and the attractiveness of the exhibits.
The government is also satisfied that the fair has played an extremely useful role in the re-establishment of overseas countries in the Canadian market. The fair has been used

by many overseas manufacturers, not only to establish trade connections in Canada and in the United States during the post-war period, but it has become the means of inducing a good many foreign and commonwealth companies to establish plants in this country.
However, in spite of the unremitting efforts of the trade fair administration and of the Department of Trade and Commerce generally, the fair has not lived up to expectations as a medium for the direct promotion of Canadian exports. Three or four years ago, in response to an appeal from me that the fair would close unless there was a greater measure of Canadian participation, Canadians did exhibit in greater numbers. But enthusiasm soon waned, and in this year's fair Canadian participation, apart from prestige exhibits by some very large Canadian companies and provincial and municipal exhibits, is very limited indeed. The conclusion one must draw from the experience of the past eight years is that a trade fair of the kind we have been running in Toronto is not of much value to Canadian exporters.
On the other hand, while the fair has made an outstanding contribution to the re-establishment of overseas countries in the Canadian market and thus has indirectly aided Canadian exports, it does not appear to have fulfilled the hopes of those who believed that the fair could become a more or less permanent market place. Our experience has been that, to a large extent, overseas exhibitors use the fair to make initial contacts in Canada and then turn to other methods of trade promotion which are more natural to the Canadian environment, including exhibitions in other fairs such as the Canadian national exhibition, as well as industry exhibitions of one kind or another. In the post-war period it was highly desirable to have a fair just for this purpose of repairing commercial connections. On the other hand, this does not seem to offer a solid base for an annual trade fair under government auspices and with government financial support.
For these reasons the government has decided that the Canadian international trade fair has fulfilled its purpose and fulfilled it well and should now be discontinued.
This decision will, I know, cause some disappointment. I can assure the house that there is no change in the government's view as to the desirability of stimulating two-way trade with our customers. The trade fair was one of Canada's main contributions to this end during the post-war period. It has been an outstanding success. We shall now bend our efforts in other directions and I hope with the same success. For example,
[Mr. Campney.l

the Canadian government will this year be exhibiting in 15 trade fairs, and exhibitions of one kind and another in 13 different countries. In this competitive world we cannot wait for the customers to come to us; we must carry our merchandise to the buyer in his country, just as we expect that he will continue to bring his merchandise to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has made a statement that, I take it, was at least in part prompted by the question I asked him on this subject several days ago. The international trade fair has been an extremely useful institution in these recent years. It has been a good advertisement for Canada. It has helped to create good will for Canada with other countries, and it has provided a meeting place not only for private citizens engaged in trade but also for officials at government levels from various countries with which Canada seeks to stimulate her trade.
I should like to express regret that the government has found it necessary to reach the decision the minister has announced today.

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, based on the statement which he has just given to the house. If the province of Ontario were willing to contribute a substantial sum of money, would the federal government reconsider its decision not to continue the trade fair? I know definitely that a large number of industries from Europe were brought to the trade fair. They are now established and are doing very well. They are producing products that were not produced here before. There is no doubt that the trade fair has 50433-286J

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

speechtext:
As a matter of fact, that
would be the logical conclusion from the speech made last night by the hon. member for Eglinton. He spent a great deal of time -101 minutes to be exact-railing against the government and against the Minister of Defence Production in particular, and railing against the bill that is before the house. But toward the end of his speech, in one of his many attempts to conclude his remarks, he said:
Mr. Speaker, the position of Her Majesty's loyal opposition is this, and I emphasize it again. We support the continuation on a permanent basis of the Department of Defence Production.
Well, if they support the continuance of the Department of Defence Production on a permanent basis, that is exactly what this bill calls for, and I presume therefore they will vote for the second reading of the bill.

Of course, true to Eglinton form, the hon. member went on and said:
We are prepared to give the government what powers are adequate to meet any proven existing need, or any that can be measured within the foreseeable future under present conditions, bearing in mind that parliament is never far away and can be called at any time if the government needs it. According to our view, these powers must be clearly defined-
And they are defined in the bill, as a matter of fact-

That is not part of the
quotation.

-and must be commensurate with a proven need. So far as we are concerned there will be no wholesale abdication on the part of parliament to satisfy a ministerial appetite for power.
Those sentences, Mr. Speaker, are like the whole speech; they are so wordy that one cannot be quite sure what they mean. But I admit that in those latter sentences there is a possible basis for a vote against the measure, as there was in the first sentence I quoted a moment ago a possible basis for a vote for the measure. So our hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party are once again going both ways.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Good old socialism.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: The Minister of Fisheries is wrong so often that I am beginning to wonder if there is not something wrong with what I am saying, in view of his endorsation of my remarks.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Well you might.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Despite that concern, I
would point out that we were told last night that we must not stand for concealment, that we must not stand for secrecy, that we must not stand for any infringement of the rights of parliament, and that we must not stand for any curtailment of the principles of freedom. Yet what we are doing is not being done behind closed doors. There is no concealment about it; there is no secrecy about it. We are right out in the open, dealing with a measure to lay down the rules and to lay down the basis under which defence purchasing will be done. So far as we in this party are concerned, we believe in responsible government; we believe in parliament laying down the rules for the executive departments of government to follow. That is what this bill does. This bill does not leave
Defence Production Act the question of defence purchasing in a vacuum. It lays down the rules by which defence purchasing will be carried on.
We think it is the responsibility of parliament to lay down these rules. If there are some clauses in the bill that hon. members do not like, it is their responsibility when we reach those clauses to move any amendments they may feel to be necessary. But to oppose the whole proposition of there being a set of rules, of there being a statute to govern defence purchasing, is, I suggest, the height of irresponsibility. If the hon. member for Eglinton meant in his 101-minute speech last night that his party was going to vote against this measure, I ask them: What is their alternative? How do they propose that defence purchasing should be handled?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: It was said very plainly last night but apparently you did not listen. It was said about three times.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I remember listening with great pain to every word that the hon. member uttered last night, and even though it was adding to the pain I looked through his speech again today in Hansard-I still say that if he is opposed to defence purchasing being carried on by a department regularly established by a statute, he has not presented any alternative. I hope some speaker in his party who will be limited to 40 minutes will be able, in that lesser amount of time, to tell us what alternative the Progressive Conservative party has unless, of course, in the end they are really going to vote for second reading after all.
As I see it, Mr. Speaker, the truth of the matter is that the bill will continue to repose in the elected government of the country, a government responsible to the people of Canada, the power to direct and, if necessary, to control industry in the national interest.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Excellent socialist doctrine.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: And that is what my hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party do not like.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: When they rave and prate about freedom what they mean is freedom for private industry.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
The minute they see any government, even if it is a private enterprise government, bringing in legislation that proposes some direction of private industry in the name of the people, boy, they trot out all the words, all the cliches and use all the

Defence Production Act time they can to rail against such a proposition. The hon. member for Eglinton had great pleasure last night quoting various remarks that have been made about this legislation by the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) as well as by others. I was waiting for the hon. member for Eglinton to give certain quotations from the Minister of Defence Production which he seemed to overlook. I am sure he is not unaware of these remarks of the minister because they were made at an earlier stage in the debate on this measure in response to questions asked by the hon. member for Eglinton. I refer to statements made by the minister as recorded on pages 1993 and 1994 of Hansard of March 14, 1955. In answer to one question that the hon. member for Eglinton put to the Minister of Defence Production, the minister said:
In the last war there was great pressure for textiles that were needed to clothe the troops. One particular textile mill refused to make cloth for the services on the ground that it did not like to do business with the government. It had the facilities and should have contributed its bit to the government program but it was more profitable for that mill to refrain from government work and to serve the domestic market which was also short of material.
When the hon. member for Eglinton objected that that was an example from the days of world war II and the minister should get up to date the minister said this:
But it might occur tomorrow. For instance, we are going into the far north to build a great project under conditions of considerable stress. Suppose our steel fabricating companies say, "Sorry, we do not like that type of work; we are going to use our facilities to build something else".
I maintain that we have a right to insist that those facilities be used for that early warning line which we believe is urgently needed, whether the steel companies prefer to do something else or not.
Then over on page 1994 the Minister of Defence Production is recorded as saying:
I seriously suggest that I can think of firms in Canada-not in the steel fabricating business- that I would not be too sure would willingly give up their domestic business in order to do defence production business.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Eglinton, who had unlimited time and could have quoted at length, did not bother with these quotations from the Minister of Defence Production which point out the need in the national interest for legislation of the kind that the government now asks parliament to keep in force. Of course the hon. member for Eglinton was not here in 1939 so he would not be expected to quote from anything the Minister of Defence Production said on that occasion. But it is relevant to the question before us, and I think we should

remind ourselves of what the then minister of munitions and supply said in reply to a question from the then member for Weyburn, now premier of Saskatchewan, the Hon. T. C. Douglas, as reported at page 179 of Hansard for September 12, 1939. This is what the minister said:
The provision of 5 per cent was put in the last act after a good deal of consideration as a minimum return for the service rendered, but it was one which men of considerable experience believed to be unworkable. I can say to my hon. friend that from that day to this the defence purchasing board has done its very best to place contracts on that basis and has used every pressure that could be brought to bear in the form of patriotism and so on, but to date it has not succeeded in placing a single contract on that basis.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
These statements I have quoted, which seriously condemn the ethics of private enterprise, are not remarks that we socialists make on street corners. These are statements made on the floor of the House of Commons by the Minister of Defence Production. If he feels there are circumstances such as these with which the government must be in a position to cope in the national interest, I suggest it is the height of irresponsibility for the member for Eglinton to say that the government should be denied this kind of legislation.
I could not help but feel that a good deal of the 101-minute speech of the hon. member for Eglinton last night was by way of a personal attack on the Minister of Defence Production. I do not blame him for that. I have had occasion to attack the minister frequently during the past 13 years, and I shall probably continue to do so as long as he and I are both here. But, Mr. Speaker, I cannot help but think that if that same Clarence Decatur Howe, instead of entering parliament, had remained in private industry and had become a great captain of industry with great powers, able to influence and direct great sectors of our country's economy, able to push men here and there and do all sorts of things as a great captain of industry, he would have been a hero in the eyes of the Tory party.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Not a chance.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: But when he wields power in the name of democracy on the basis of responsibility to parliament and responsibility to the people, oh no, that is a different story. He is interfering with the great basic concept of freedom because he enunciates the principle that the national interest should come before the interests of private firms. That is the position of my Tory friends.

Mr. Speaker, we will deal with the matter of the extent of our defence expenditures when we come to another subject. We feel, therefore, that this department of government should be continued. We want the government to do something about health and welfare. We do not leave it to the cabinet in a vacuous state, we set up a Department of National Health and Welfare. We want the government to do something about agriculture, so we set up a Department of Agriculture and we lay down rules and regulations. I suggest it is parliament's job not just to say we will turn these powers over and we will review them in two, three, five or ten years. No, it is parliament's job to maintain a constant scrutiny of a department of this kind. It is parliament's job not only to examine the expenditures of the Department of Defence Production, but to examine closely the expenditures of the Department of National Defence. I do not think it is necessary in connection with this bill, especially after the case put up by the hon. member for Eglinton, to speak at great length. So far as the arguments are concerned, I think the hon. member did not leave much to be said. Furthermore, I find myself in substantial agreement with the position he took on the bill. It may be that the hon. member did not state specifically how he and his party would vote on the motion for second reading. I do not suppose any one of us can tell; and it is none of our business, anyway, until the vote is taken.
But on March 14, at the resolution stage of the bill, I think that all on this side of the house took a reasonable position and made

a reasonable request of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe). The stand we took then is exactly our position today; and I wish to put that categorically so that there will be no misunderstanding. I assure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that before I sit down I will tell him where we stand on the vote to be taken shortly-at least I hope shortly.
In the first place we support the provisions of clause 1 in the bill. In my judgment it is only right that the salary of the Minister of Defence Production should be in line with those of other ministers. It appears that at the time of the revision of the Salaries Act some action was taken; and we have no objection at all-in fact we want the Minister of Defence Production, so long as there is a separate minister, to have a status in keeping with that of his colleagues in the cabinet. So that there is no quarrel in that regard.
In the second place we are in agreement with the minister when he says that the Department of Defence Production should be made a permanent part of our government set-up. We agree that the employees of his department should be able to count on something like permanent status. I can understand how unsettled they might be without a status that could be considered permanent. It is only right therefore that they be permitted to count on such permanent status. As Canada grows in population and in prestige, in what has become an unsettled world, our security will be more and more bound up in an efficient Department of Defence Production.
Let me hasten to say that I do not make that statement because I think in terms of war. I do not. Nor do I make the statement because of any belief that we have no hope of achieving peace in the world. I do say it however because the facts of the world situation tell us quite plainly that we are going to have to make almost constant defence efforts and preparations perhaps for many years to come. Even if peace does come- and I sincerely hope and pray that it will, and very soon-we will not even then be able completely to relax in our defence efforts. Nor can we hope to depend upon other countries to do our defence producing for us. And so we support the minister in his request that the department be made, looked upon and considered in every respect as a permanent part of our government set-up. We do express the hope, of course, that the time will come, and come speedily, when that department will not need to be as busy as it has been and as it is now. And I would

The third important point is this: We believe that the minister and his department should be clothed with powers sufficient to enable them to furnish Canada with all the materials needed to secure us as best we can be secured. We realize that the powers as set out in the act of 1951 are very broad and very sweeping, and to anyone unaccustomed to considering the transfer of such powers to government they appear a bit frightening. I do not think that at any time during the emergency of war this parliament and its members have looked upon the transfer of such powers as are outlined in this bill with anything but grave misgiving-even in a time of war and stress.
How, then, should we look upon them now, in a period, not of war, but surely one of great danger, but not one considered to be of great emergency? I think we can all be excused for looking upon such transfer with some misgivings, and not with the apparent joy with which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre seems to view the transfer. Once those powers are transferred on a permanent basis, as a parliament we could exercise no effective check over them.
I draw my hon. friend's attention to the growing number of items in the estimates that come before us from time to time bearing the notation "S", with a circle around it. When we are in committee of supply and reach one of those items, what do we do? We leap right over it, for the simple reason that these are statutory provisions, clothing the minister of the department with powers this parliament has no right to question. And that is something to which I believe careful attention should be given.
Any time anyone says that all we need to do is exercise vigilance, I would say to him that all the vigilance in the world will not exercise a check on those powers permanently transferred by statute, because by statute they are given, and only by statute can they be returned. And if a majority sits in the House of Commons and refuses to bring in a statute for their return, or to support such a move, then how in the name of common sense can any vigilance be exercised or any review be made of such power which in any way could be considered effective?
I ask the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to consider that, when he says so glibly that he is not afraid. Let me point

And I say to the house that there are certain parts of our country where there is compulsion of fear, and where that compulsion of fear can be exercised in unrighteous ways and in ways that are good for the government but certainly not good for the people.
All one has to do is to travel through the province of Saskatchewan today to find out about compulsion of fear. All he has to do is hear some of the businessmen in that province talk about the fear under which they have to carry on, and how unsettled they are.

One out of seven is a very fair percentage. However, it is difficult for any of us to say with any degree of assurance that we are right; that the powers as set out in the act of 1951 are excessive to the needs of the government today. I would not like to say so at all. I know, as I said, they are broad and they are sweeping and they are such as to make it possible to create that compulsion of fear in the country. But at the same time I say it may be that the situation in which we live is such as to demand those. I would not like to say to my hon. friend the minister that I believe they are excessive at all. I do not believe they are excessive at all in times of emergency or of great danger. In times of war or in times of strong threat of war, I believe the Department of Defence Production requires vast powers. We have recognized that in times past and we have given vast powers for the reason that we expect them to act quickly and effectively, and they must have them if they are to work fast and effectively. In time of danger parliament has granted more powers, even more powers than may be used; for in my judgment there is always uncertainty about what the department and the government might have to deal with.
War is not what it used to be by any means. In these days no one is inclined to abide by the Marquis of Queensbury rules with respect to war. As the minister said last night, we do not have the leisure or the time these days to get ready for war. It simply strikes like lightning, fast, and in most unexpected ways and places. Therefore we are not inclined to beef too much about the powers in the bill of 1951, although one contrasts, and cannot help contrasting, the powers in the Canadian bill with those in the British bill.
I draw your attention to the contrast which was made last night by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). When one looks at those and makes a comparison he finds that the powers in the Canadian act do appear to be excessive. Would the minister or anyone else say that the United Kingdom government has been any less efficient in preparing for defence than we have been? I should like to have a statement on that. It appears to me that the United Kingdom has been most efficient and has done a good job, and one

does not hear any complaints about it. When you go back to the days of the Labour government in Britain you find that they did not resort to the kind of transference of powers to any department that we have here, and that we are asked to make on a permanent basis.
The minister admitted last night that there are powers in the Defence Production Act which he has never used. Probably he will never have to use them. I sincerely hope not. I hope he will get that kind of cooperation in the Dominion of Canada that will make it unnecessary for him to use those powers. When it is essential in the interests of our security to invoke those powers, then we think they should be made available to him to use. We are not kicking about that. Our position in this respect was well put by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more) on March 14, when we were discussing the resolution. I just wish to quote briefly what he said as recorded at page 2003 of Hansard:
What conceivable chance has the opposition of obtaining a review of this act once it is passed and goes into the records? What assurance have we that 10 years from today there will be in charge a man who will be as sane, as wise and as responsible as the present Minister of Trade and Commerce? I do not hesitate for a minute to say that I think what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has done, with the tremendous powers he has had during the last few years, has been admirable. I do not see how a man could have done any better. But let me say this. We do not often find a man like the Minister of Trade and Commerce; we do not find more than one in about every million. We therefore must take precautions to see that the country shall be reasonably safe no matter what kind of minister gets into that position.
I say amen to that. We cannot always count on having the same kind of person in the department as we have now. Therefore we must be careful. That is as far as the agreement with the minister goes. But when he asks today that the powers in the defence production bill of 1951 be made permanent or continuing powers, then we have to part company with him.
Both the minister and the Prime Minister have said, in different ways it is true and at different times, that there are powers in the bill that should not be continuing powers. Why then does the Prime Minister, who introduced this measure, ask that section 41 of the act be repealed? Section 41 is that section of the act which terminates the unusual powers in the midsummer of 1956. Neither the Prime Minister nor the Minister of Defence Production has advanced one single good reason why the unusual powers should be continuing or permanent powers; not one. I listened with great interest to what the minister said last night, and I read
Defence Production Act over again what he said and marked it in Hansard so that I would not make any mistake. He did not give one single good reason to show why he needed to have those powers made continuing or permanent powers. He did convince me with his logic that the department should be made permanent, and we agree with that. But, as I say, he did not give one single good reason to help us to believe that these unusual powers in the act should be made permanent and continuing powers. I searched carefully through what the minister said yesterday and I could not find a single thing that would make me believe that I should vote for the repeal of section 41 of the act, except of course that the department should be made a permanent one and that the employees should be given permanent status.
I have already said that we are prepared to support the two things that the minister has asked for, namely, permanent status for the department and permanent status for his employees. But we are unalterably opposed to any action of this parliament to give permanent status to the powers that should only be given to a minister or a department in times of emergency and great danger, and for those times. We made that quite clear on March 14, too.
While we were considering the resolution we thought, from what the Prime Minister said at that time, we had some reason to believe the government would bring in some amendment to the bill before it was taken up again, which would make it necessary for the government to bring this act before parliament periodically for complete review. After three months we are now told by the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) that he wants the bill as it is or not at all, which means that he has closed his mind to the reasonable request we made on March 14.
We have not heard anything from the Prime Minister, and I am wondering why, as did the hon. member for Eglinton. I think the Prime Minister should make a statement on this bill and tell us why in the three months that he has had to consider the matter he did not bring in some provision to successfully replace section 41 and make it mandatory upon the government to bring the act in for periodical review by parliament so we could have a check on it.
We have heard nothing from the Prime Minister and I suppose we must assume from that that our request for inserting such a provision in the bill as I have suggested, a terminal provision or a provision requiring that it be submitted periodically to parliament for review, is not to be met and that he has closed his mind on that matter as well.

I speak for my group in this house when I say that we have approached this whole matter with a view to finding out what is right. We believe that it is right that parliament should never delegate powers to any individual, group of individuals or department without surrounding the granting of those powers with adequate checks and balances as insurance against the misuse of the powers. I think that that is the principle of the rule of law and the supremacy of parliament. We believe that this parliament is the repository of all the sovereign authority of the people of Canada and therefore we have no right to dispose permanently of any of those powers. Even if we hand over powers only on a temporary basis we are obligated not to do so without a provision for terminating the grant or the requirement that parliament be given an opportunity to review and to make full scrutiny of the way in which the powers have been used.
That is what we want now. I think our request is reasonable and fair. What is the right thing for us to do on this motion for second reading? I think the right thing for us to do would be to support those things which the minister requires and which are right, but also to serve warning that when the bill is in committee we will move for the deletion of clause 2, which repeals section 41 of the act, and offer an amendment to make it mandatory upon the government to bring the act back to this house for complete periodic review and scrutiny. We are unalterably opposed, may I repeat, to the granting to the minister and his department of unusual powers on a permanent basis, and against that we will continue to fight.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with keen interest last night to the remarks of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and today I listened with interest to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). I find myself somewhat in agreement with the last speaker with reference to certain things in this bill which has been moved for second reading on behalf of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent).
I am surprised that the Prime Minister has not been in the house during this debate.
I realize his responsibilities are great, but I can think of no greater responsibility after having moved this motion than to be here to safeguard the rights of parliament which, in the years that have passed, have been championed so often by those who sit to your right.
I observed that the hon. member for Eglinton spoke at some length and with some


enthusiasm about this issue as it concerns parliament itself, as it concerns the rights of members, and as it concerns the rights of the Canadian people. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said that the hon. member for Eglinton had spent 101 minutes. I have been in this house for a long time and in the last 30 years in this parliament I have never known anyone who has talked so much and so long and said so little as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. During the last session he spoke over 700 times. One week I observed that during the five days he spoke 30 times. I sometimes think that as he belongs to a party that will never have the responsibility of government he feels that he can talk as long as he wants and say as much as he wants, as often as he wants.
I cannot quite understand the admiration he has for the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). He was almost offering bouquets to the government today. I have heard the hon. member in the past speak quite differently, when he was more critical of the government than he was today. This seems to suit the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre quite well. He says that if the Minister of Trade and Commerce had been in business he could have shoved men around. How he could have shoved men around! Now he wants to lay down legislation so that someone in the minister's place can shove all men and all industry in Canada around. They are not satisfied to be just a little dictator in connection with one industry; they would like to nationalize all the industries of Canada.
I have great regard for the Prime Minister, who has moved this motion, and I have keen regard for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I realize that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has had long experience in engineering. Since I have been in this house I have become convinced that there are two professions, that of Your Honour, the law, and that of engineering, which are best fitted for parliamentary service. A lot of engineering must be done in political tactics and careful observation must be given to see that the rule of law is maintained.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has rendered good service to this country. In fact he almost became a hero in the wartime boom. His ability is undoubted and indeed his integrity is unchallenged. He has been a most fortunate and happy victim of favourable circumstances so far as prosperity is concerned.
There is another thing I want to say about this bill. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is said to be usurping powers, but he cannot usurp powers because he has the

power to do as he likes under this act. In all fairness I want it understood that I am not speaking personally, but this is laying a pattern which is dangerous for the welfare of this country. That is why I submit that in connection with an issue as important as this the Prime Minister should be here during this debate.
We of Her Majesty's loyal opposition want to hear from the Prime Minister on this issue. We want to know where he stands. Last night the Minister of Trade and Commerce was quite indignant and spoke with some heat about the rumour that there was a difference of opinion in the cabinet in connection with this matter. I notice that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and the Prime Minister are conspicuous by their absence today, and there are not very many ministers in the house either.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to be disturbed at all by the cackles and growls from the back benches on this issue, because this is an important issue. This is one which concerns the life of this house. This is one which concerns the supremacy of parliament. This measure is unnecessary today. No doubt the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre enjoys it. You could not put his type of policy into practice without it. You have to have all these powers in order to nationalize industry and socialize industry across Canada. It is a socialistic move, as far as the government is concerned. The government has never been embarrassed. But, Mr. Speaker, no government of this country has ever been embarrassed by the policies of the Conservative party in times of emergency. All through the years our record has been clear in that regard. We have
Defence Production Act never stood between the government and necessary authority in time of trouble. Our record is clear, back over the years. In the years of the 1914-1918 war this party suffered because of its stand in that regard. We would not be worthy of our place here if we did not follow that attitude. The Liberal party has at times refused to take the action it should have taken, as when it refused to provide for airfields in 1938. But today where is the emergency? Is the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance now studying it?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
May I ask my hon.
friend a question? Why are we spending $300 million or $400 million to build early warning lines across Canada?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: If there were a greater emergency than there was when you said this should not be continued, why are you reducing your over-all expenditures this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: We are not.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Yes, by some $20 million or $30 million. Why is the expenditure less?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: What percentage of the total estimate is $20 million or $30 million?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I know, "What's a million?" In this case it is, "What is $20 million anyway?" Under this act you can deal with $100 million without coming back to us. Yes, what is $20 million in the kind of expenditures that this government carries on? They have increased their expenditures all through the years on civil account and for a time reduced them on defence; yet they come to the house now and tell us now that there is such an emergency in connection with defence that we have to have powers that five years ago we would not touch at all. The Prime Minister himself, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce also, said as far back as 1951 that some of the powers sought in this bill are special powers and should not be of a continuing nature.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Now read the rest of it. That is half a sentence.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: The Minister of Trade and Commerce himself said that it should not be of a continuing nature at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I believed that it should be continued as long as the emergency continued.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Does the Minister of Trade and Commerce not intimate by that that we will be in an emergency as long as we live?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
As long as he is minister.

Defence Production Act

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I point out to my hon. friend that in 1947 I liquidated an act with powers equal to this, because I did not think it was needed any more. It would have remained liquidated except for another emergency. When this emergency is through we may wish to liquidate this act. I do not propose to be told now by any hon. member just when I will liquidate it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I realize that, but somebody may liquidate you some day, at election time. I do not know whether it is a falsehood, but we hear rumours that the minister is going to retire, and in fact we even hear rumours that the Prime Minister is going to retire. What is going to happen then? Is this a deal that has been made? Has the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) made a deal with the government so that there will be a coalition between the socialists and the Liberal party in this country? I wondered why he was so happy today. Somebody is going into the Senate. He may be going into the cabinet.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: When my hon. friend takes over, he can repeal it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: The Minister of Trade and Commerce is a great champion of free enterprise and he knows, as well as he knows I am looking at him, that he does not need this par-manent bill. No emergency needs a permanent bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: If you think that, you do not know what is going on in the world.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: He has said that when the fact that it is not needed has appeared he can liquidate it as and when he wishes, not when parliament wishes. Mr. Speaker, I have listened for a quarter of a century or so to speeches in this parliament-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: And learned nothing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: You have not learned much in the few years you have been here. I have listened to my hon. friend for many years talking about the supremacy of parliament and saying, "Trust the people", and I have heard him say that when a government fails to trust the people the people fail to trust the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: The people do trust us.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Forty-eight per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: When they trust you, you can do something about this legislation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: It is like the answers we get from the other side of the house. They say, "Look at the support we get in the country; that is why we can liquidate acts when we please; that is why we can hold parliament in contempt; that is why we do not need to listen to the opposition". A trend has been developing in this country so rapidly since this government has been more or less power-drunk, in the last several years, that one would think no one had any right in this house to criticize the government in any way. If we use that term "for emergency", why does not the Prime Minister or the Minister of Trade and Commerce take us into his confidence? If they are not satisfied to let the public in the gallery know, they can call a private session, a war session, and let us know what this emergency is. They have the War Measures Act, if required, and they have all the powers they need without half the powers of this act. If they need it at all, then they should tell us why, and not say, "We are a free enterprise party, but we want to make this permanent. We are not at war, but we want a plan for an emergency that has passed, so that we will have a pattern for socialism for the future for our friends to the left."

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I am glad to know the emergency has passed.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I am speaking in terms of an emergency that needs the powers under this bill. I am speaking of the use of the term "emergency". This party has not criticized the government for the amount of money it has spent even though we have criticized the way it has been spent in some respects; we have not criticized the war budget. We do not intend to criticize the war budget. We have told the people that we need taxation, that people must pay taxes in order to defend this country. There is no monopoly on sincerity in that regard. But there is no monopoly on the rights of parliament. There is no monopoly on those who would destroy the powers of this house. I say in all sincerity that this, in the guise of a war emergency, is a blueprint of a perfect pattern for a socialistic regime. True, the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce has more confidence in his party and his free enterprise policies than to believe that he or the Prime Minister would use it as a socialistic plan. But why do they want to make it permanent? Why have it after they are gone?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: We have confidence in our judgment.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
We have heard that said before by certain people in Europe who ran everything in a one-man show. I cannot understand why a party that has the powers that this

party has must have a form of an act that is a pattern for a totalitarian state. All they need to do is to have the socialists elected and get into this house, and then they would be able to put that into effect.
The pattern is made to order. I think that is why the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre appreciates it so much. I have never seen him laud an act of the government as vigorously as he has lauded the bill before us today. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence Production have both said that these are unprecedented powers, powers that should not be continued. But now they are continuing them with, I say again, less of an emergency staring us in the face than there was when they said they did not need to be continued.
Why do they need to be continued in this manner? Is there any minister or any member within the sound of my voice who will say for a moment that if we pass this legislation now for a period of a year we will not do so again next year if the emergency remains? Why this permanency, why this long-term socialistic pattern even for an immediate emergency, if the Minister of Defence Production is right?
The minister attempts to frighten us today by suggesting that there is an emergency. I do not know what the emergency is, Mr. Speaker, but I think I have a right to know something about it. A lot goes on in this department and in several other departments that I do not know anything about because questions often go unanswered or are sidetracked and debates are juggled and fumbled so that we only get a few days on one debate and then it is postponed in order that the government may get through the session as easily as possible, and with the least embarrassment.
Let the government take the house into its confidence. If we are facing an emergency, if we need this measure let us know it. If conditions are that bad then let them clear the galleries, clear the press gallery, call a secret session of parliament and tell us why they cannot face the emergency unless they have this authority. We can count on the Canadian people to support us, exactly as they did all during the war. Every industrialist, every workman in the country played the game just as the soldiers did.
But I do not believe the Minister of Defence Production has decided that he will nationalize the whole economy of Canada. Why then does he seek this power? Why have the power to do it? No wonder the socialists to my left are lapping it up. They would be delighted, in the same way as the socialists in the United Kingdom who almost ruined the
Defence Production Act country and who recently suffered a terrible defeat. If they need powers of this kind then let the minister tell us in private session, if necessary, or in committee that the situation is so serious that he needs the power to take over real or personal property at whatever price he decides, that he needs the power to make contracts and then turn around and break them if he wishes to do so. He has that power under the act. Let him tell us that the situation is so serious he needs power to examine the books of a corporation and then refuse to believe the books; that he needs power to name an agent to run a business when he does not think it is being run properly, even if only part of that business has to do with war production; that he needs power to force a company to enter into a contract and to take over the company if it refuses to sign a contract. If they sign a contract and make a deal he can refuse to pay them what he said he was going to pay because he thinks they have made too much money. If he likes the colour of their eyes he can pay them more than he agreed to pay them.
All these things can be done under this bill. If the minister's agent at Ottawa thinks the bookkeeper of a corporation has had more expenses than he considers reasonable, the agent can set the figure to suit the minister. These things sound ridiculous, but the bill is ridiculous. These are the powers vested here. Are these the reasons the cabinet benches are so empty today? Are some members of the cabinet not satisfied? Some conspicuous members of the cabinet are not here now, and they did not look happy when they were here. There are many members in the party to your right, Mr. Speaker, who must squirm when they read that if a person refuses to make a contract with the government the minister can make him enter into a contract or surrender his business. They must squirm when they see that if the person makes such a contract and loses money he must regard the position as being the same as if he had tendered on the job.
I do not believe for a minute that the Minister of Defence Production, as long as he is in office, would use this legislation to injure Canada. I do not believe he would use the act to nationalize industry. I know his inclinations in that regard quite well. I do not believe he would use the act to tell a candidate he could not run for the Conservative party.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I believe he would.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I think he would.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I do not believe he would say to a person, "I do not think you can fulfil
