Defence Production Act this contract if you are going to be a Conservative candidate." I do not believe he would use the act for political purposes. I do not believe he would tell them not to contribute to the Conservative party and I know he would not tell them to contribute to the Liberal party. But under this legislation he has power to do almost anything he likes. In fact I should like to know what he could not do under the act. He cannot take a man and throw him into jail without a trial, as he could under the War Measures Act. He cannot tell the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) that he has to quit parliament and go and dig ditches.
But, Mr. Speaker, if I am the head of a corporation which is engaged to some extent in defence production, and if I make a contract with a labour union-let the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre tell his labour friends about this-under the act the minister has the power to break the contract made with that labour union, whether it means 10 cents an hour more, 20 cents an hour more or guaranteed annual wages. That is a pretty far-reaching power. It can be done at the whim of the minister. It can be done by the action of his agents. As I watch the actions of the government and look at this legislation I am more than ever convinced that what Lord Acton said is still true, that all power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely.
When power is being sought that is not needed can you blame us, Mr. Speaker, for being critical? I do not like to be critical of the government. I realize the responsibilities they carry. I realize the Minister of Defence Production has carried a great load of responsibility. We have long since recognized his sound ability in many respects, as have most Canadians. In fact before he was in parliament he was employed by the party to which I have the honour to still belong, and he performed great service for us. If we had known he was going to enter politics we might have persuaded him to join us.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Then the bill would be O.K.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
But, Mr. Speaker, that is beside the issue. Let no one think I am attacking the Minister of Defence Production or the Prime Minister, but it is our duty as members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition to see that the supremacy of parliament is maintained, and we are not going to be sidetracked by the anxious and hungry desires of the socialists to our left or the whims of a minister who seems to think all power is safe as long as it is in his own hands.


This is not good enough, Mr. Speaker. This bill says that if the officers or directors of a corporation are not doing a service as the agent of the minister thinks they should, and if by their conduct they are going to fail to complete a contract as they should, then they can be dismissed. The innocence of their failure must be proven by them. The old axiom has been changed, and no longer under this act are you innocent until proven guilty. If the government does not like you, you are guilty until proven innocent.
As I said at the outset, I am not a lawyer. Neither is the Minister of Trade and Commerce. But I am amazed that the Prime Minister of Canada, who has been the head of the law society of Canada and is such an eminent member of the bar, would ever allow an act like this to be made permanent. In time of war no one in this house and few in the country would not be satisfied to pay their debts like the boys and girls have paid who lost their lives; that is not an issue. Surely we can trust the people. But why introduce an act with all these powers merely because a minister says, "You should trust me; I liquidated one act before and I can liquidate this." Should we sit idly by and wait and wonder whether or not the act will be liquidated, or the minister liquidated by an election? Elections are uncertain.
Does anyone think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-of course I know it is but a dream, and there is little chance of the hon. member sitting where the Minister of Trade and Commerce now sits- would ever let go of these powers? He would laugh and hang onto them like a bulldog to a bone. They would be the blueprint for his socialism. He could say to anyone sitting in the opposition that his party did not introduce this act. It was brought in by that great free enterpriser the Minister of Trade and Commerce. This act was brought in by that great Prime Minister who had been head of the bar association and was an eminent lawyer. This act was brought in by the party that received the greatest majority in the history of Canada. This act was brought in by the party that talked free trade one day and attacked it another. This act was brought in by the party that talked about the supremacy of parliament from one side of their mouth and destroyed it from the other. This is the party that talked about the individual rights of parliamentarians, and then ignored them one after another. The Minister of Trade and Commerce today has demonstrated his qualities more than ever by the fact that he says he alone should liquidate it; that he should be trusted to liquidate it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: He did not say that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Quote him accurately.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Take the plugs out of your ears and listen.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Perhaps I did add a word, but the meaning is still the same. In this instance the Minister of Trade and Commerce did say he liquidated one before and he thought he should be trusted to liquidate this one as he saw fit.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: My hon. friend told the house the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that only he could liquidate it, and of course he said no such thing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I stand corrected. He did not say only he could liquidate it, but he said he would be the only one who would liquidate it. He said he should be trusted to liquidate it. I realize that someone else could liquidate it, but the chief liquidator is the man who has the power. I realize there is a clear-cut distinction. In fact the hon. member, being a member of the press for so long, is closer to being a lawyer than I am, but the spirit of the answer is the same and indicates the same socialistic trend.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: You are just confused.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: If I were confused I would not seek any help from the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), who has just interrupted.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I am glad of that, too.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I know, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will not likely tell his labour friends just what these powers mean. I say quite seriously that the minister or his agents have power under this act to annul or repudiate any contract between a company and a labour union, when even part of the work of that company is for defence purposes. This same power could be used to repudiate any contract made with a government, any contract made with a municipality, or any contract made with a province. In fact the minister has power under this act to repudiate even a statute of this parliament.
Where are those old champions of the supremacy of parliament? Where are those who have worshipped at the shrine of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mackenzie King? Let them go back and read the speeches of 1921 and 1925, as well as others. Why, Mr. Speaker, those men would almost turn over in their graves if they saw their successors now so hungry to take these powers and make them permanent. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce will do nothing else, will he not rise in his place today and say that these powers are only needed for defence purposes,
Defence Production Act and that if we think the act is that strong they will only ask for them for three years or five years? I believe that is longer than the Minister of Trade and Commerce intends to be here. According to rumours it is longer than the Prime Minister expects to be here. It will be longer than that before the Minister of Fisheries can ever hope to be prime minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: You will be gone.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I was here before you were.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: You can console yourself.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I hope I am not here then. I do not wish any of you ill luck, but I do expect to be around for a long time. I know some of the younger people, the youngest of them all, will have lived a long time before the Minister of Fisheries ever assumes the role upon which he casts his eye sometimes.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: You have been here 30 years and learned nothing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
You have done pretty well. I do not intend to say much more, but I am amazed and shocked, and I say in all sincerity that never in my experience in this house, which now covers 30 years, have I ever witnessed a spectacle like this. I have never witnessed the spectacle of a government seeking powers such as are being sought in this act and trying to make them permanent.
Another thing no less conspicuous is the fact that the Prime Minister himself, the sponsor of the bill, has not been here to listen to a single word of the argument for or against it. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) has not been here either. I can tell by the weary and worried face of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) that if it were not for the sake of decency he would probably rather not be here.
So, Mr. Speaker, last night when the hon. member for Eglinton was charged with uttering a falsehood I believe the hon. member deserved the sympathy of the house. All one had to do was look at the faces of those opposite to realize that there must have been many of them who were worried. I have watched the faces of cabinet ministers for a long time and I cannot help but think there must have been rumblings in the mulberry bushes over this bill.
I would urge the Prime Minister to come back into the house and tell us what he thinks of this bill. Tell us why he has moved it. Tell us why he has to have powers he is never going to use. Tell us why all these spectacular powers are going to be conferred.

Defence Production Act
Is there an hon. member within sound of my voice, any hon. member among this great mob of government supporters, who cannot see the real intent? Are they content to sit idly by and listen to the gibes of the Minister of Fisheries and the rumblings of some other backbenchers, such as the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) and others who, so long as they pound their desks or interrupt Conservatives while they are speaking, believe that they are paying homage to the all-powerful Liberal government? Some of them act like socialists and are admired by socialists, whether they are socialists or not.
I hope there is no collusion between those who sit to my left and the government; because while hon. members sitting to my left have no chance alone, they perhaps feel that if they clothe this government with power through this bill, then they will be making some sort of negative contribution to the economy of this dominion.
This government has taken many powers it did not need. It has done so, not only for the general purpose of having power, but-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: We thought the hon. member had finished his speech.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Well, I believe my time has almost expired. I realize, of course, that what I say will not matter very much. If this bill is going to pass it will not matter whether one talks for 40 minutes or 20 minutes. It would matter very little, in fact, whether individual members spoke at all. The government seems to think that it matters very little what kind of deal they make with the provinces and the municipalities. It will matter very little except as to the personnel, the man who is going to administer the act. I have complimented the present minister much more than he has complimented me, and I believe more than the Minister of Fisheries. He is a lawyer, too, and-

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: No, thank God.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I was going to say that if he is, then he must be a very poor one. But I say in all sincerity that if this act is made permanent we will have it that way forever in Canada. Sound, sensible and honest people, people who believe in the free enterprise system, have made this country what it is, despite what is said by hon. members sitting to my left. Here is a pattern made to order, a blueprint ready to be followed by the wildest socialists we have ever seen, if they wish to use it.
I urge the Prime Minister, who is not present this afternoon, and I urge the Minister of Trade and Commerce to do some quiet and private thinking in the quiet hours


tonight. Let them go home and conclude that perhaps they can do with three years. Perhaps it would be safe to have five years. Perhaps it would be safe to make it ten; or will they just leave it so that no matter who comes into power they can do as they like, and instead of having parliament supreme it will become negative and almost useless because they do not like parliament anyway.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not been 30 years in the house so perhaps I may be excused if sometimes I am somewhat puzzled. I have been under the impression that we are discussing a bill to amend the Defence Production Act, a bill of two clauses. But as I listened to the two wings of the Conservative party yesterday and today I find that they are concerned with the actual provisions of the Defence Production Act itself.
I would like to know if either of these groups is going to have the courage to implement the complaint they made last night and again today, by bringing in a measure to amend the powers set out in the Defence Production Act. Are they going to have the courage to call for a reduction in defence expenditures? They have changed their line. Now they are no longer the voice of doom, predicting communist aggression almost every other Thursday; now they have decided that there is no urgency. Are they going to bring in a motion to reduce defence expenditures?
I listened last night, as long as I was physically capable of doing so, to the hon. member for Eglinton, and I did not discover a single argument, except his argument against the powers that are in the act and have been in it ever since it was passed. It may or it may not be that the government requires these powers. But I suggest that it is frivolous irresponsibility on the part of members to stand up in this house, on the pretext of an amending bill of this sort, to object to the powers in the act, if they have not the courage to offer amendments to that act themselves. It is frivolous irresponsibility, and I challenge the spokesmen for the Conservative and Social Credit parties to bring in an amendment which would curtail these powers which they consider so extremely dangerous.
We have been told for the last two years, time and again, from both wings of the Conservative party, that we have to watch out, that communist aggression is lurking just around the corner. If that is so, then presumably Canada requires defence. And if Canada requires defence, then we have to

purchase materials for that defence. I do not mind being called a socialist; I am a socialist. In fact I do not care if you call me a communist. But I will say this, that the welfare of Canada and of the Canadian people must take precedence over any private interest.
Let me point out to members of the Conservative and Social Credit parties that, as has been pointed out before, it was private industry that went on strike in 1939. I would tell the honourable and loquacious member for Dufferin-Simcoe that it was not labour that went out on strike; it was capital that went on strike in 1939, and that was prepared to let Canada go down the drain if they could not have the terms they wanted from the government and people of this country.
I suggest that these hon. members who have been objecting should name specifically the powers they would take away from the Minister of Defence Production. Let us have it spelled out so we can understand easily. What is it he is no longer to be allowed to do? If they are not prepared to come forward with that information, then let them tell us just what is the sinister aspect of making this department permanent.
I heard it suggested here last night at appalling length, and again this afternoon, that it is not possible to do anything with the Department of Defence Production once this amending bill is passed. That seems to me a confession of failure on the part of members of the House of Commons, because every year the operations of that department are under review by parliament. Every year every act of parliament is under review, potentially. Any member in the house who feels that there is an act vesting the government with powers they should not have is free to bring in an amendment.
Do we hear them doing it? No; we hear them getting up on the basis of a small amending bill and making an attack on the Department of Defence Production, and they have not the courage to make the attack openly. They have not the courage to state specifically that certain powers must be taken away.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that if we have an emergency as we are told we have-[DOT] and I have not the slightest doubt that some time, even in the remaining few days of this session, members of the Conservative and Social Credit parties will be warning us about the dangers of communist aggression-then we must face the realities of this modern world. We must realize that we have to prepare for that emergency ahead of time. It is no use to say that we will give the
Defence Production Act minister these powers when the first hydrogen bomb drops. If there is any way of stopping that bomb from dropping he has to have power to act now.
I do not know how he has exercised his power in the past. I have been told that he has exercised it well. He may have done it well or otherwise; but somebody has to exercise this power in the paramount interests of the Canadian people so as to override the selfish interests for whom the parties to my right and left are such eloquent spokesmen.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the various speeches that have been made I must admit that there is very little left to say. However, one way of emphasizing certain points is by repetition, and I want to emphasize very clearly the stand enunciated by our leader, the hon. member for Peace River, a few moments ago.
Before doing that, may I say I was rather intrigued by the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. But I must say I was not surprised at his socialistic views favouring national control. We expect this, and expected him to commit his group to support a measure that is centralizing control of industry in the national government.
I trust the government appreciates the fact that it is sponsoring control over private industry, which meets with such enthusiastic support from our socialist friends.
Another statement the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre emphasized was "we believe in responsible government". Who does not? We in this group are as jealous of our belief in this principle as any group in this house. But at the same time we also realize it is possible to have too much government. We believe the people of Canada are entitled to enjoy a wide degree of individual freedom and individual rights, and we shall oppose any action by any government, national, provincial or municipal, which takes away these rights in times of peace, in times of non-emergency.
The only criticism I have to offer of the speech of the hon. member for Eglinton is that he left very little for the rest of us to say. Another statement that rather tickled my fancy last night was one made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in describing this bill. He said, "It is a very simple bill". Well, it is simple; it is one of the shortest, if that is what he means by simplicity, that have come before the house this session. There is an old saying that many good things are done up in small parcels. It is equally true that many highly explosive articles can also be done up in small parcels.
4548	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act
The sad part of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is that it is another one of those package deals that we have been getting so often this session. Clause 1 deals with raising the salary of the Minister of Defence Production. I do not think there is any quarrel with that. So far as we in this group are concerned, we believe there should be a permanent Department of Defence Production. We are firm in our belief that whoever heads the department should be paid the salary that is being paid to other ministers of the government.
While saying that and agreeing that the Department of Defence Production should continue, we should also like to pay tribute to the right hon. member who has occupied the position of Minister of Defence Production for the past few years. He has been paid a good many compliments during the last few hours, but a few more might be in order.
I believe the people of Canada, from one end to the other, are well aware of his personal contribution to the business of government and to the wonderful developments that took place from 1939 to 1945 which made it possible to win the war in which we were engaged. When the minister steps out of office, as he is bound to do sooner or later, to take that well-earned rest to which he is entitled, I often wonder where the government of the day will find two men to fill the position which this one man is filling at the present time.
While we are in favour of a permanent Department of Defence Production, we cannot agree with the arbitrary powers over industry in time of peace that are given by this act. We admit that in time of emergency, or in time of war, rigid controls are necessary, and I am sure we would have no objection to invoking the War Measures Act, or any legislation necessary to make this act effective. These measures could be invoked by parliament on very short notice.
We maintain that Canadian industry should not be under the heel of any dictatorship; and I am afraid, despite other words to the contrary, that is what is being set up in this house at the present time. I was going to read some of the sections to which we take such strong objection, but the hon. member for Eglinton read them last night. They are sections 23, 24 and 27. To my way of thinking they are most objectionable, but I recall that last night the Minister of Trade and Commerce interjected and said, "Did you read section 25?" Well, I read section 25, Mr. Speaker. It says the party concerned shall be compensated. Well, surely to goodness no one believed that any department of government would confiscate goods and plants, if necessary, without compensation.


These are dictatorial powers, and the least I can say about them, using language that is not too strong, is that they certainly are not democratic powers. In wartime and in peacetime industry has done a good job under free enterprise. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of this group, I would say let us keep it free until an emergency calls for some drastic regulations.

They were so far out of line with reality on that occasion that when they get out of line again, as they have done this afternoon, I suppose none of us should be surprised. Their stand on some of these issues shows much more clearly than I can in a few words just why they are unlikely to be entrusted by the people of Canada with the direction of the affairs of this nation.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that it might be of some value this afternoon for me to outline the course of the debate on the resolution which preceded the bill. That debate commenced on March 10. It was opened by the Prime Minister. It has already been pointed out by several hon. members that this measure has been sponsored throughout by the Prime Minister. As I said, he opened the discussion on March 10, though yesterday he failed to open the debate on the motion for second reading of the bill. As yet he has not taken any part in the debate at this stage.
Speaking on March 10 the Prime Minister admitted that the Department of Defence Production had been set up to meet an emergency which had been brought to a head by the fighting in Korea. He admitted also that at that time, which was three months ago, the peak of Canada's defence program was past. As a reason for this present measure he stressed the production of aircraft and electronic equipment, but admitted that there were certain powers under the Defence Production Act which were not being used. I quote from page 1905 of Hansard of March 10, where the Prime Minister had this to say:
There are other powers which are not being used at this time but which were placed there because they were considered to be essential in dealing with any emergency which might arise and which might interfere with the regular production and procurement of what was necessary to build up our forces and to discharge our commitments to our associates in this joint undertaking.

After the Prime Minister had spoken, members of the opposition pointed out various facts in connection with the Defence Production Act. For example, we referred to the statement made by the Minister. of Defence Production on March 2, 1951, a little over four years ago. He was referring to the request made by the hon. member for Peace River and myself. Then the minister said it was impossible to separate the powers, that they could not draft an amendment to separate the powers. That is done in the house at every session. In fact the minister's own bills, the essential materials (defence) act, the munitions and supply act and the Defence Supplies Act all have different provisions, and there has never been the slightest difficulty about varying the provisions from bill to bill.

The minister made one other excuse. He said the powers taken in this act were no greater than those in the Expropriation Act. How he reached that conclusion is quite beyond my ability to understand. The Expropriation Act provides a procedure for filing a plan in a land registry office, expropriating the land, and then compensation, but there is nothing in that act such as is contained in this act giving the power to appoint controllers, to seize a man's business, conduct investigations into his business, and all that sort of thing.

The fact is, Mr. Speaker, this is a bill tailored to suit this one minister. I point out that under section 5 all the powers given to the minister can be exercised by an appointee. It reads:
The minister may authorize any person, on his behalf and under his control and direction, to do any act or thing or to exercise any power that the minister may do or exercise under this act.
The minister says that his appointees and his department must have these wartime powers. On March 14, 1955, just three months ago, at page 1996 of Hansard, we find this:
We did not take action under the powers. The powers were there, however.
Here we have a case of the greed for power of one man. Parliament is asked to bend the knee, just as business in Canada has been asked to bend the knee to this minister. It is high time this tyranny was stopped. We offered to agree that the minister could keep the powers if they were made for a period of time, say for two or three years, when they would again be subject to review. We offered to endorse the bill if the powers were restricted to such products as aircraft and electronics, instead of having a definition of defence supplies so broad it covers everything produced in this country. We suggested that the government go over the bill carefully and remove the sections that they themselves admit should not be continuing. We have been met with a refusal of each one of those suggestions. The minister's stand today-not the Prime Minister, and we want to hear his stand-is all or nothing.
The war has been over for 10 years, Mr. Speaker. The emergency powers act was dropped last year, and the Prime Minister admitted that act should be dropped. The Defence Production Act, in its present form, is not needed today any more than the emergency powers act was needed last year. If the minister cannot operate this Department of Defence Production without these powers, then let him give up that portfolio and devote himself to the Department of Trade and Commerce. He has a full-time job in selling Canada's wheat and looking after some of these trade problems he is having with the United States. I suggest the minister take on that job and let somebody else handle the defence production department.

Defence Production Act
If there were a new minister there is not one member in the Liberal or C.C.F. parties who would suggest that he be given these wide open powers the present minister is demanding. If a new minister asked for powers of this nature he would be laughed out of the house, and properly so. Because it happens to be this minister, the members of the Liberal and C.C.F. parties are prepared to give him all the powers for which he asks.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say there has been a lot of emphasis on the need for building up our defences, and a lot of emphasis on the need for defence production. That is all very true, but the strongest weapon of this country is not defences or defence materials; the strongest weapon of this country is freedom. This act takes freedom away from the Canadian people. For that reason there is no excuse for this government asking that the act in its present form be accepted by the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: It is with considerable hesitation that I take part in this debate-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Why bother?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
-but for reasons which the hon. member who has just interrupted would perhaps not appreciate, I feel I should take part, because I consider the subject matter to be one of the most important to come before this parliament in recent years, or likely to come before it in the near future.
On this occasion we are debating a piece of legislation which strikes at the very roots of our democratic system. We are being told, of course, that it is quite innocent legislation, not only innocent but necessary. It is necessary because at this time we find ourselves in a world which is divided into two factions. We are told that we must keep ourselves strong militarily in order to survive. These, of course, are facts and I do not disagree with them; but they are not justification for throwing away bit by bit the liberties and freedoms which we have set out to defend.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to take part in this debate because I realize my capabilities are perhaps not such as will measure up to the magnitude of the problem. This is a subject which would require the full powers of a Churchill, a Burke or a Lincoln to appreciate and expose the full significance of the insidious tendencies exhibited in this legislation.
It has been urged that it is necessary to make permanent the Department of Defence Production, and I do not think there are many members in the house who would quarrel with that suggestion. So far as we

can see into the future it seems likely that we will require to procure large amounts of munitions. Therefore in the view of most of us it is justified that the Department of Defence Production should be permanent. I, for one, am perfectly willing to go along with that suggestion.
The first clause in the bill would increase the minister's salary. That would appear to be an innocent clause, to which no one objects so far as I know.
However, when we turn to the second clause we find that not only would it make permanent the Department of Defence Production, but that it is a package deal. Tied up with the objective of making the department permanent we find that it also makes permanent these extraordinary powers now contained in the act.
The minister has suggested that it is impossible to bring about the desired result in any other way. He even led us to believe that he was open to suggestions as to how this package deal could be avoided. If the minister was sincere in that suggestion, then I am sure there are many who could offer suggestions to him to solve his dilemma.
As was said by the previous speaker, the sections of the act to set up the department on a permanent basis could be enacted in their present form. On the other hand those sections in the act which would make permanent these extraordinary powers vested in the minister could have a time limit imposed upon them. That is one suggested solution. Another solution would be simply to extend the life of the present act but to impose a time limit of four or five years during which it would operate.
Then an entirely different approach could be made. The present act followed the Defence Supplies Act. I think the purpose of the procurement of defence supplies could be met if an entirely new bill were introduced which would set up the Department of Defence Production in much the same way as every other department of government is set up. That act could come into force at the expiration of the present one; and when the present act expires the Defence Supplies Act would automatically come back into force. It could give the power required by the Minister of Defence Production for the procurement of defence supplies.
I should like to quote briefly from what was said by the minister in the house on March 2, 1951, when the Defence Production Act was under debate. This is what we find at page 839 of Hansard:
By and large, these are the powers that are now contained in the Defence Supplies Act-

He was speaking o f the powers in the present Defence Production Act.
-which, hon. members will notice, is only being suspended during the life of the present proposed act. Other powers are of an extraordinary nature but fitted to the extraordinary circumstances of today.
That is, fitted to the extraordinary circumstances existing in 1951. Then I should like to quote what the minister had to say when the Defence Supplies Act was being debated in the house in 1950. These are his words, as reported at page 3633 of Hansard:
The threat seems to be made from all sides of the house that this legislation will be defeated. I will say at once it is all right with me if it is defeated because I will at least get full marks for having tried to remove from the statutes legislation that is far too dictatorial and stringent for peacetime. I have tried to retain from the existing legislation only those powers which are reasonable peacetime powers for carrying out the procurement duties involved in the defence of Canada.
I am curious as to why the minister realized in 1950 that the powers required for an all-out war effort are not suitable for peacetime, and why he now turns his back on his viewpoint of five years ago.
It is a fact of history that most civilizations of the past, setting out to make sure that they would continue into the future, taught that their sole danger was from without, and that they could be destroyed only by attack from without. History teaches us, however, that in nearly all cases civilizations have ceased to exist not as the direct result of attack from without but because of rot from within. And the principles upon which they first prospered were whittled away to such an extent that eventually those civilizations collapsed from within.
That is my fear at the present time. Many people take the shallow view that progress is inevitable and democracy is permanent. I see no reason why our civilization or our way of life should be considered immune from the forces which have existed throughout history. I feel there is a real danger that in our efforts to defeat totalitarian attack from without we will destroy our civilization from within. To my mind that is a great threat.
Many people realize, too, that when we give extraordinary powers to any minister- and I am not casting any reflection upon any particular minister or any particular individual, because I make due allowance for human nature-such extraordinary powers tend to corrupt. I should like to quote briefly from a book entitled "Faith and Freedom", by Barbara Ward. This quotation is found at page 202, in these words:
After the French revolution, thoughtful men were profoundly impressed and disturbed by its brief showing forth of total dictatorship.

They came to believe that any attempt on the part of the community to concentrate all power- moral, political and economic-in the hands of the state and to use that power to bring about an earthly Utopia could result only in unmitigated despotism and the defacement of humanity. They appealed to the older traditions of Europe-incorporated in the political systems of Britain and America-to the separation of powers, to the supremacy of law over government, and governed, to the idea of a religious loyalty which transcends the state, and to a modestv in political aims which could recognize that paradise cannot be built and ordinary men deified by violent acts of state.

speechtext:
No. There is a great deal to be learned from history, and I commend a study of history to anyone with such aims. Anyone who would preserve our present civilization can certainly learn from the mistakes of the past.
Behind all the constitutional checks imposed by medieval theory upon the governors of society lay the perception that unchecked power will be abused. Power is never exercised in vacuo. It is exercised by men. Expose them to the possibility of unlimited domination and they seize it: all but a minute fraction of them will deteriorate in the process as the ego grows by what it feeds on. This is the lesson of all history. This is the fundamental reason why human freedom fills so brief a span in the long development of man.
I do not consider for one moment, Mr. Speaker, that this is something to be taken lightly, or that it is only a case of getting a bill enacted by this parliament within a certain length of time, or anything of that sort. It should be remembered that all dictatorial powers which get into a position of control do so by a gradual and insidious process. It behooves us to guard the ramparts of freedom, not only by military arms and by efficient military forces, although they are necessary, but by safeguarding the principles on which our free civilization and our democratic system of government are based.
I should like to read a quotation from a book entitled "The Urge to Persecute" by A. P. Davies. The quotation may be found on page 139, and reads as follows:
It is always "little by little". As James Madison warned us, "There are more instances of abridgement of the freedom of the people by gradual and silent encroachments of those in power than by violent and sudden usurpations."

Defence Production Act
Many peoples and many civilizations have realized their mistakes when it was too late. They looked upon trends that were taking place as necessary ones that were not especially dangerous, but before they realized it they had gone beyond the point of no return.
I should like to read another quotation from "The Urge To Persecute". It will be found on page 111:
The time to deal with tyranny is before it becomes established; once entrenched, it maintains itself with ease against those who could have ore-vented it. This, unfortunately, is the lesson which, again and again, the human race has learned too late. The little courage which it would have taken to stop a would-be tyrant before he had achieved power was more courage than his prospective victims could muster. They wrung their hands, they muttered their dismay to one another, they whispered their fears-but they did not act. They were too afraid.
My suggestion, Mr. Speaker, is that now is the time to act. There can be no valid justification for the extraordinary powers which the government would have us give to the Minister of Defence Production. The purposes of the Department of Defence Production in the efficient procurement of supplies for the defence forces can be achieved without such extraordinary powers. I continue with the quotation:
Yes, evil ascends unchallenged, not because it is unrecognized as evil but because good people are not brave enough to check it. It is all in those six short words: "For goodness dares not check thee."
This United States writer goes on to say:
That is what has been happening in our own country in the last few years. Not that we are yet ruled by tyranny; we are still a free people who elect our own government. But we are indulging tyrannous elements that operate under the protection of our government. In the eyes of many, what these elements are doing is not alarming; if there is wrong in it, it must be condoned because of the end it serves-or which they think it serves. They do not see that this is how tyranny has always been excused-until too late!
I should like you to pay special attention to these words:
No would-be tyrant announces that his aim is power; he is the protector of the people, warning against their enemies, the popular champion of a plausible crusade, a persecuted hero, intrepid and dauntless amid the host of his detractors. Thus he presents himself, and although his character is plainly manifested by his deeds, thus he is accepted -by too many until it is too late.
I believe that is exactly what is happening now. This extraordinary legislation is being justified in the name of the protection of freedom. It is being justified because the minister admittedly has to work under difficulties, and the procurement of sufficient defence supplies is naturally a great problem.


For all of these reasons attempts are being made to justify this very extraordinary legislation.
The quotation I have read is only one man's opinion, it can be argued. It can be said that it does not carry any more weight than anybody else's opinion. The man who wrote it happens to be an authority on the study of present-day history, and I think his opinion is worth while. Nevertheless we can test the validity of the opinion. We can consider for a moment the statements that have been made in support of this legislation. It has been said that this legislation is necessary because it is for the good of the employees of the Department of Defence Production, who want to know that there is permanency in their jobs. It has been said that it is a good thing because it will help in the procurement of munitions and supplies for the defence of freedom, which is a worthy cause. It is justified on the flimsy suggestion that you cannot have a Department of Defence Production without extraordinary powers. Those extraordinary powers are justified by the statement that they will rarely be used, that likely they will not have to be used in the future so there is no harm in having them since they will not actually be brought into operation.
That reminds me that our most recent dictator came to power under constitutional law, using the ordinary and recognized methods of gaining power to a great extent. Adolf Hitler came to power in Germany by having a large group of his party elected to the parliament of Germany in election after election, supported by the socialists. I think they are familiar with what nazism stands for.

I admit that the party was backed by the industrialists, who went along because they wanted to curry favour with what they considered the strongest party. They realized their mistake, as many people do, when it was too late. As I was saying when I was interrupted, the nazi party in Germany came to power by using the accepted methods of politics in that country to a great extent, until eventually by negotiation with

other parties and by dealing with the communists and by the use of other methods they obtained a majority in the German parliament.
Hitler gained his first important position of power by the passage of a bill in the German parliament. It was a simple bill, and it was said that its provisions would not need to be used and it would do no harm. Just as we have been told now, it was said that the rights of parliament would not be disturbed or lessened. When I listened to the explanations given by several members of the government-I say this in all sincerity- they unwittingly and by absolute chance reminded me of Hitler's statement in the German parliament when he introduced the enabling bill of which I am speaking. I took the trouble to look up his speech, and these were Hitler's words on that occasion:
The government will only make use of these powers in so far as they are essential for carrying out vitally necessary measures. Neither the existence of the Reichstag nor that of the Reichsrat is menaced.
It would not interfere with either houses of parliament.
The position and rights of the president remain unaffected. It will always be the foremost task of the government to act in harmony with his aims. The separate existence of the federal states will not be done away with.
In other words it would not interfere with the rights of the provinces.
The rights of the churches will not be diminished and their relationship to the state will not be modified. The number of cases in which an internal necessity exists for having recourse to such a law is in itself a limited one.
The law is justified because the occasions on which you could possibly use it are few and far between.
All the more, however, the government insist upon the passing of the law. They prefer a clear decision.
Every sentence in that statement has a familiar ring.

It is because I believe in the democratic way of life which was established by our forefathers that I think it behooves us to protect that way of life by retaining our parliamentary system which has been gained with such great difficulty. I feel sincerely that these things must be protected, not only by means of war or military defence but also by the exercise of unspectacular and tedious methods through the use of free speech and seeing that no undemocratic bits of legislation creep into our code of law.
This piece of legislation is being enacted because there is a threat of communism, and we must make ourselves strong against that threat so we may bargain from strength. The vast expenditures of treasure and energy which are being made for defence purposes by the western world are being made to defend our way of life. It is just as necessary to defend our way of life in less expensive ways.
In closing I should like to sum up this point of view by another quotation from a book from which I have quoted already, called "The Urge to Persecute" by A. P. Davies. This quotation will be found on page 212. The book was written by an American, and it looks at the problem from the American point of view. It is a point of view that applies not only to the United States but to Canada as well, and to the whole western world. He says:
If our cause is just, if we are worthy of it. if we serve it wholeheartedly, the laws of God are with us.
We have not sufficiently remembered this. It is not that we have done badly in all respects. In some we have done well. We have fed the hungry, succoured the needy, defended the oppressed, resisted the aggressor, pled for peace. But we have also distrusted-many of us-our great traditions and we have lost confidence in our freedoms.
Communism is the enemy. But we cannot defeat it by remaining as we are. We cannot shorten the struggle. We cannot subdue it by force of arms without inviting-even if we won- a measureless catastrophe. We must wear it down.

Defence Production Act We must resist its aggressions and be alert to its conspiracies. We must outplan it, outperform it. We must carry our way of life to a level that leaves communism a hopeless and irrelevant contender. Our truth must defeat its falsehoods, our liberty its servitude, our justice its oppressions, our compassion its cruelties, our faith its cynicism, our humanity its degradations and debasement.
We cannot do this if we lower our own standards and betray our [principles. That is why we must rebuke those who say that they are fighting communism but who are careless of our moral values. They could all too easily lose us the battle. For the struggle is not between communism and a debased democracy; that would be a struggle that we could not win. The real struggle-and the one we can win and must if we are to survive- is between communism and democracy's moral values.
Mr. Speaker, for these reasons I find it impossible to support this measure in its present form. In saying that I do not minimize in any way the importance of our military forces or the importance of having them adequately equipped. However, I do believe there are better ways of achieving that objective than what is suggested here. I believe those objectives could best be achieved by setting up a defence production department on a permanent basis like any other department of government, but having these extraordinary powers limited to those which are appropriate in a situation which is short of all-out war.
For myself I freely say that if the government would come forward with any reasonable compromise limiting these powers, either in extent or by a time limit, or finding some solution that will break up this bundle bill that is being handed to us, I would almost certainly support it, if there were no other strings attached. But I cannot possibly vote for this legislation as it now stands.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) made a thoughtful suggestion in answer to the minister. He pointed out a simple alternative in keeping with the views expressed by the minister on the 2nd of March, 1951, when he stated that these powers should not be of a continuing nature, apparently because of their absolute nature. However, there has been no suggestion on the part of the government that it intends to deviate one whit from the trend
that apparently is to be followed, of establishing for ministers of the crown and this government an absolutism.
It begins to look, from what we heard this afternoon through the press, before parliament opened, that in the department of defence as well a spirit of absolutism is coming into being. One wonders, in view of the paucity of the explanation this afternoon, whether General Simonds is about to depart from the service of this country because of a lack of sycophancy in his attitude to the government. Certainly that is but another example of the trend that is revealed in this legislation now before parliament, which in effect emasculates parliament and places the minister in a position where he is all-powerful, under a statute which places him above parliament by the extension of powers far beyond those that are necessary, regardless of what conditions may be.
The Prime Minister introduced this legislation. The Prime Minister's place is in this house, to explain why such extraordinary powers are being asked for an indefinite period into the future; why the pathways of absolute power, which was previously limited, are to become under this legislation the highways of permanence. This is a serious bill. It is one that in its simplicity looks innocuous, but on examination it reveals that continuing trend to absolute power. Under this legislation the Minister of Defence Production will have granted to him absolute power for an indefinite period into the future, uncontrolled by parliament.
As I sat and listened to the debate I waited for something other than the specious explanation given up to the present time as to the reason for the change in attitude from that of 1951.
